title: Jets Trade Hellebuyck to Devils for Mercer, Daws, Bjugstad, Picks in Blockbuster Deal
body:
Winnipeg’s franchise‑cornerstone goaltender Connor Hellebuyck was dealt to the New Jersey Devils on Tuesday in a multi‑asset trade that also sends forward Nathan Mercer, defenseman Nick Daws and forward Erik Bjugstad, along with several draft picks, to the Jets. The move comes just as Hellebuyck’s 11‑game suspension for violating the league’s performance‑enhancing drug policy expires, leaving the Jets to rely on the recently signed Stuart Skinner as their number‑one netminder for the remainder of the season.

The three‑team deal reshapes both clubs’ rosters and salary structures. Winnipeg, which has struggled to a 4‑3‑3 record without its All‑Star goalie, receives a mix of youthful depth and future assets. Mercer, a versatile forward who posted 15 points in 52 games last season, adds scoring depth and a right‑handed shot on the wing. Daws, a defensive prospect who spent most of the 2023‑24 campaign in the AHL, offers the Jets a low‑cost, left‑handed blueliner who could develop into a reliable third‑pair option. Bjugstad, a veteran presence with a history of clutch scoring, provides immediate depth in the forward group. In addition, New Jersey has included a 2025 second‑round pick and a 2026 third‑round pick, while Winnipeg adds a 2025 fourth‑rounder and a 2026 seventh‑rounder to balance the exchange.

For the Devils, acquiring Hellebuyck is a clear statement of intent. The New Jersey club has been hovering near the Eastern Conference playoff line, and the addition of a Vezina‑contending netminder could be the missing piece to push the team into the postseason. Hellebuyck, a three‑time Vezina winner and the league’s most consistent goaltender over the past decade, brings a career 2.66 goals‑against average and a .915 save percentage. His presence will not only elevate the Devils’ defensive metrics but also allow head coach Lindy Ruff to play his top defensive pair more aggressively, knowing the last line of defense is elite. The contract he carries—seven years at $57 million—fits comfortably under New Jersey’s cap ceiling, especially after the departure of forward Jesper Bratt and the trade of forward Michael Bunting earlier this month.

Winnipeg, on the other hand, faces a short‑term challenge and a long‑term gamble. Skinner, who inked a two‑year, $7.5 million extension in July, has posted a respectable 2.67 GAA and .912 save percentage in his first 7 games, but he is still untested as a full‑time starter. The Jets’ management appears confident that the blend of younger talent and draft capital will sustain the team’s competitive window while giving them flexibility to re‑tool after Hellebuyck’s departure. General manager Kevin Cheveldayoff has emphasized that the trade was “about adding depth and future flexibility,” suggesting that Winnipeg may be positioning itself for a rebuild or a re‑load, depending on how quickly Skinner can adapt.

Analysts also note the broader implications for the league’s goaltending market. Hellebuyck’s move marks the first time a Vezina‑caliber netminder has been traded in the modern salary‑cap era, signaling that teams are now willing to part with cornerstone players for a package of assets. The trade could set a precedent for other clubs with aging stars to explore similar deals, especially as the NHL approaches a new collective bargaining agreement and the market for elite goaltending talent remains thin.

Looking ahead, the Jets will need to rely on Skinner’s poise and the newly acquired depth to navigate the grind of the remaining schedule. Their success will hinge on whether the incoming forwards can translate their potential into consistent production and whether the defensive corps can tighten up without Hellebuyck’s steady presence in front. For New Jersey, the immediate test will be integrating Hellebuyck into a system that demands quick puck handling and aggressive play, while managing the salary cap to retain their core. If the Devils can harness Hellebuyck’s elite skill set, they could solidify a playoff berth and perhaps make a deep run, while Winnipeg may emerge as a more balanced, draft‑rich organization poised for a new chapter.
